etymologies.etymologyHTML: Noun dated in the 13th century AD and verb dated in the late 14th century AD; from claspe, possible modification of clapse, which is from Old English clyppan (“to grasp”). Related to English enclasp (“embrace, hold tightly in one's arms”).

definitions.definition: A fastener or holder, particularly one that clasps.
(in the singular) An embrace, a grasp, or handshake.
(transitive) To take hold of; to grasp.

quote.text: And when the Boy dropped off to sleep, the Rabbit would snuggle down close under his little warm chin and dream, with the Boy's hands clasped close round him all night long.

quote.citation: 1897, Bram Stoker, chapter 21, in Dracula, New York, N.Y.: Modern Library, →OCLC:
quote.text: The poor dear lady shivered, and I could see the tension of her nerves as she clasped her husband closer to her and bent her head lower and lower still on his breast.

definitions.definition: To shut or fasten together with, or as if with, a clasp.
